warmup.q: The reflective container wires a 14-component payment app with one JDK proxy and one Byte Buddy subclass. Roughly how many classes does that JVM load before the first payment is done?
options: About 30: the 14 components and a few container classes
About 1,000, the same as any small Java program
warmup.why: On JDK 21 the reflective start loaded 2,207 classes: 814 of them from the Byte Buddy JAR, 30 JDK proxy classes, 3 classes Byte Buddy generated, and over a hundred hidden classes for lambdas and method handles. The same app wired by generated code loaded 991. Most of a container's start-up cost is the machinery, not your components.

sections.h: A proxied call costs nanoseconds and a couple of hundred bytes
sections.html:
Start with the cost per call, measured the way Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from taught: the result returned, the input in a non-final @State field, and -prof gc for bytes. ProxyCallBench calls one fee calculation four ways. Each interceptor chain holds a single interceptor that only calls proceed(), so the numbers are the proxies' own cost, and the direct call is the baseline. One run on this course's 4-vCPU VM, which was shared with other builds at the time:

Call ns/op B/op
direct 3.2 0
generated forwarding class (this lesson) 4.0 0
Byte Buddy subclass (lesson 2) 90 160
JDK proxy (lesson 2) 112 208

The time error bars were larger than most of the scores, so read only the order. The bytes are exact and the same on every run, which is why they are the number to trust.

Where do 208 bytes come from? The JDK proxy's generated method boxes the long argument and puts it in an Object[]. The handler builds an Invocation for each step of the chain and a lambda for the target call. Method.invoke boxes the result. The generated forwarding class does the same things in its source: new Object[] {p0}, new Invocation(...), a lambda. But its whole call is plain code that C2 can inline, and once inlined none of those objects leaves the compiled method. Escape analysis, from Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis, removes them all. On the two reflective paths C2 couldn't see the whole call, so the objects stay. Don't build on that zero: as the Try it shows, one more interceptor is enough to lose it. The Kotlin twin counts the same calls in a plain loop and gets 0, 208, 192 and 48 bytes: the same order, with less of the generated class's allocation removed.

Does it matter? At 2,000 issuer calls a second, 208 bytes is 400 KB/s of garbage, next to a 120 ms network call: nothing. In a loop that prices 10,000 line items through a proxied FeeCalculator, it is 2 MB per batch. Proxy the issuer client, not the arithmetic.

try.title: Count the bytes per call
steps: Read ProxyCallBench. Predict the B/op of each of the four benchmarks before you run it.
Run it (it forks four JVMs, about 10 seconds). Then run the Kotlin twin, which counts bytes with the per-thread allocation counter instead of JMH.
In ProxyCallBench, add a second PASS to CHAIN (List.of(PASS, PASS)) and run it again. Which rows change?

code.title: ProxyCallBench.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l03.demo; import net.bytebuddy.ByteBuddy; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.MethodDelegation; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Setup; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.profile.GCProfiler; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import workbench.container.l03.InterceptingHandler; import workbench.container.l03.Interceptor; import workbench.container.l03.Invocation; import workbench.container.l03.SubclassBridge; import java.lang.reflect.Method; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named; /** * One fee calculation, called directly and through the container's three kinds of interception. * Every chain holds one interceptor that only calls proceed(), so the numbers are the proxies' own cost, * and direct() is the baseline to compare against. * Short runs on a shared machine: read the order and the bytes, not the decimals. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 150, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 150, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class ProxyCallBench { public interface Fees { long feeMinor(long amountMinor); } public static class PlainFees implements Fees { @Override public long feeMinor(long amountMinor) { return (amountMinor * 29 + 500) / 1000; } } static final Interceptor PASS = Invocation::proceed; // does nothing but carry on static final List<Interceptor> CHAIN = List.of(PASS); /** A copy of the forwarding class RegistryGenerator writes for an intercepted interface. */ static final class Fees_Proxy implements Fees { private final Fees target; Fees_Proxy(Fees target) { this.target = target; } @Override public long feeMinor(long p0) { return (Long) new Invocation("Fees.feeMinor", new Object[] {p0}, CHAIN, () -> target.feeMinor(p0)).proceed(); } } long amount = 12_000; // non-final: the JIT can't fold it Fees direct, jdkProxy, byteBuddy, generated; @Setup public void setup() throws Exception { direct = new PlainFees(); Method fee = Fees.class.getMethod("feeMinor", long.class); jdkProxy = (Fees) Proxy.newProxyInstance(Fees.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] {Fees.class}, new InterceptingHandler(new PlainFees(), Map.of(fee, CHAIN))); byteBuddy = new ByteBuddy().subclass(PlainFees.class) .method(named("feeMinor")) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration().filter(named("intercept")) .to(new SubclassBridge(Map.of(PlainFees.class.getMethod("feeMinor", long.class), CHAIN)))) .make().load(PlainFees.class.getClassLoader()).getLoaded() .getConstructor().newInstance(); generated = new Fees_Proxy(new PlainFees()); } @Benchmark public long direct() { return direct.feeMinor(amount); } @Benchmark public long jdkProxy() { return jdkProxy.feeMinor(amount); } @Benchmark public long byteBuddy() { return byteBuddy.feeMinor(amount); } @Benchmark public long generated() { return generated.feeMinor(amount); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(ProxyCallBench.class.getName()) .addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) // the same as -prof gc .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-10s %9s %9s %9s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error", "B/op"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var time = r.getPrimaryResult(); var bytes = r.getSecondaryResults().get("gc.alloc.rate.norm"); System.out.printf("%-10s %9.2f %9.2f %9.1f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), time.getScore(), time.getScoreError(), bytes.getScore()); } } }

alt.title: ProxyCallBench.kt
alt.html: package workbench.container.l03.demo // ProxyCallBench.java times these calls with JMH, which needs Java classes in this lab. This twin // makes the same four calls from Kotlin and counts the bytes each one allocates with the JVM's // per-thread allocation counter, after a warm-up so the JIT has compiled them. import net.bytebuddy.ByteBuddy import net.bytebuddy.implementation.MethodDelegation import net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named import workbench.container.l03.InterceptingHandler import workbench.container.l03.Interceptor import workbench.container.l03.Invocation import workbench.container.l03.SubclassBridge import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.lang.reflect.Proxy interface KFees { fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long } open class KPlainFees : KFees { override fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long) = (amountMinor * 29 + 500) / 1000 } private val chain = listOf(Interceptor { it.proceed() }) // does nothing but carry on /** The shape RegistryGenerator writes for an intercepted interface. */ class KFeesProxy(private val target: KFees) : KFees { override fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long = Invocation("KFees.feeMinor", arrayOf(amountMinor), chain) { target.feeMinor(amountMinor) }.proceed() as Long } private val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean private var sink = 0L // results go somewhere the JIT can't ignore // inline: every use gets its own call site, which sees one class, as each JMH benchmark does private inline fun bytesPerCall(call: (Long) -> Long): Double { repeat(200_000) { sink += call(12_000L + it % 3) } // warm up: let C2 compile the path val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes repeat(100_000) { sink += call(12_000L + it % 3) } return (threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before).toDouble() / 100_000 } fun main() { val fee = KFees::class.java.getMethod("feeMinor", Long::class.java) val jdkProxy = Proxy.newProxyInstance(KFees::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(KFees::class.java), InterceptingHandler(KPlainFees(), mapOf(fee to chain))) as KFees val byteBuddy = ByteBuddy().subclass(KPlainFees::class.java) .method(named("feeMinor")) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration().filter(named("intercept")) .to(SubclassBridge(mapOf(KPlainFees::class.java.getMethod("feeMinor", Long::class.java) to chain)))) .make().load(KPlainFees::class.java.classLoader).loaded .getConstructor().newInstance() val direct = KPlainFees() val generated = KFeesProxy(KPlainFees()) println("%-10s %8.1f B/call".format("direct", bytesPerCall { direct.feeMinor(it) })) println("%-10s %8.1f B/call".format("jdkProxy", bytesPerCall { jdkProxy.feeMinor(it) })) println("%-10s %8.1f B/call".format("byteBuddy", bytesPerCall { byteBuddy.feeMinor(it) })) println("%-10s %8.1f B/call".format("generated", bytesPerCall { generated.feeMinor(it) })) println("(checksum $sink)") }

try.expect: direct and generated show 0.0 B/op, byteBuddy 160 and jdkProxy 208 (or very close), every run. Times jump around, with errors larger than the scores on a busy machine, but direct and generated stay within a few nanoseconds and the two reflective paths are far slower. With two interceptors every row but direct allocates more. In one run the reflective rows grew by 32 bytes each (one more Invocation, to 192 and 240), and generated jumped from 0 to 128 B/op: with the longer chain, escape analysis no longer removed its objects. That is why Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis said to show escape analysis in demos and never assert it in tests. Change the chain back afterwards. The Kotlin twin prints 0, 208, 192 and 48 bytes per call.

sections.h: At start-up the reflective container loads Byte Buddy and generates classes
sections.html:
The per-call cost is small. The start-up cost is not. StartupLadder packs the demo app into a JAR and starts it in fresh JVMs, counting -Xlog:class+load lines by their source: as Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it did. On JDK 21:

setup                       loaded  archived  run-time  ready ms  wall ms
reflective + Byte Buddy       2207       953       156      1029     1307
    parsed from byte-buddy.jar 814, JDK proxies 30, defined from bytes 3, hidden 123
generated registry             991       834        51       266      418

The 1,216 extra classes are all machinery. 814 come from byte-buddy-1.18.17.jar: the library has to load its own type model, its matchers and its class writer before it can write one subclass. The 3 classes defined from bytes (source: __JVM_DefineClass__) are what it wrote: SettlementService$ByteBuddy$... and two $auxiliary$ classes, the @SuperCall callables for settle and audit. Then 30 JDK proxy classes (__dynamic_proxy__). Only one of them is the issuer proxy. Every annotation you read through reflection is an instance of a proxy class the JDK generates for that annotation type, so getAnnotation(Component.class) and isAnnotationPresent(Timed.class) generate classes too, and Byte Buddy uses a few proxies inside. The 123 hidden classes are lambdas and method handles; since JDK 18 core reflection itself runs on method handles, so every reflective call path adds some.

Each of those classes is found, parsed and verified, and then run in the interpreter, because nothing is hot yet (From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2). That is why ready (from the first line of main to the first payment done) was 1,029 ms against 266 ms. The machine was busy and the times moved by a factor of two between runs. The reflective start was always several times slower, and the class counts barely moved.

None of this is Byte Buddy being slow. It is doing at every start what a compiler could have done once.

try.title: Count what each start loads
steps: Read StartupLadder (the Kotlin twin runs the first two rows). It generates the registry, compiles it with javac, packs container/build/cap4/app.jar, and starts the app in child JVMs.
Predict the loaded column for the first two rows, and the parsed from byte-buddy.jar count for the generated registry.
Run it. It takes about 10 seconds. Ignore the last two rows until section 5.

code.title: StartupLadder.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l03.demo; import workbench.container.l03.Container; import workbench.container.l03.Interception; import workbench.container.l03.RegistryGenerator; import workbench.container.l03.demo.app.DemoApp; import javax.tools.ToolProvider; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.jar.JarEntry; import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream; import java.util.stream.Collectors; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** * Starts the demo app in fresh JVMs: wired by the reflective container, then by a registry generated * "at build time" (here, at the start of this demo), each with and without a dynamic AppCDS archive. * Class counts come from -Xlog:class+load and barely change between runs; times change a lot. */ public class StartupLadder { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("--reflective")) { // the child JVM's entry point long t0 = System.nanoTime(); String result = DemoApp.run(new Container(DemoApp.COMPONENTS)); System.out.println(String.format("ready: %s in %.0f ms", result, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6)); return; } Path demo = location(StartupLadder.class); // build/classes/java/demo Path out = Files.createDirectories(demo.getParent().getParent().getParent().resolve("cap4")); // container/build/cap4 Path jar = buildApp(demo, out); List<String> classPath = new ArrayList<>(List.of(jar.toString())); for (String entry : System.getProperty("java.class.path").split(java.io.File.pathSeparator)) { String name = Path.of(entry).getFileName().toString(); if (name.startsWith("byte-buddy-") || name.startsWith("kotlin-stdlib-")) classPath.add(entry); } String cp = String.join(java.io.File.pathSeparator, classPath); Files.writeString(out.resolve("classpath.txt"), cp); // for the AppCDS and AOT cache commands System.out.printf("JDK %s, app and class path in %s%n", Runtime.version(), out); System.out.printf("%-26s %7s %9s %9s %9s %8s%n", "setup", "loaded", "archived", "run-time", "ready ms", "wall ms"); String reflective = StartupLadder.class.getName(); String generated = "workbench.container.l03.demo.gen.GeneratedStart"; row("reflective + Byte Buddy", List.of(), cp, reflective, "--reflective"); row("generated registry", List.of(), cp, generated); for (String[] setup : new String[][] {{"reflective", reflective, "--reflective"}, {"generated", generated, ""}}) { Path jsa = out.resolve(setup[0] + ".jsa"); // training run: the archive is written at exit Files.deleteIfExists(jsa); run(List.of("-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=" + jsa), cp, setup[1], setup[2]); row(setup[0] + ", AppCDS", List.of("-XX:SharedArchiveFile=" + jsa), cp, setup[1], setup[2]); } } /** One logged run for the class counts, then one quiet run for the times. */ static void row(String name, List<String> flags, String cp, String main, String... args) throws Exception { List<String> logged = new ArrayList<>(flags); logged.add("-Xlog:class+load"); List<String> lines = run(logged, cp, main, args); List<String> sources = lines.stream().filter(l -> l.contains(" source: ")) .map(l -> l.substring(l.indexOf(" source: ") + 9)).toList(); long archived = sources.stream().filter(s -> s.startsWith("shared objects file")).count(); // "(top)": AppCDS long proxies = sources.stream().filter(s -> s.equals("__dynamic_proxy__")).count(); long fromBytes = sources.stream().filter(s -> s.equals("__JVM_DefineClass__")).count(); long hidden = sources.stream().filter(s -> !s.startsWith("jrt:") && !s.startsWith("file:") && !s.startsWith("shared") && !s.startsWith("__dynamic") && !s.equals("__JVM_DefineClass__")).count(); long byteBuddyJar = sources.stream().filter(s -> s.contains("byte-buddy-")).count(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); String ready = run(flags, cp, main, args).stream().filter(l -> l.startsWith("ready: ")).findFirst().orElseThrow(); long wall = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-26s %7d %9d %9d %9s %8d%n", name, sources.size(), archived, proxies + fromBytes + hidden, ready.replaceAll(".* in (\\S+) ms", "$1"), wall); System.out.printf(" parsed from byte-buddy.jar %d, JDK proxies %d, defined from bytes %d, hidden %d%n", byteBuddyJar, proxies, fromBytes, hidden); } static List<String> run(List<String> flags, String cp, String main, String... args) throws Exception { List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(flags); cmd.addAll(List.of("-cp", cp, main)); Arrays.stream(args).filter(a -> !a.isEmpty()).forEach(cmd::add); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); List<String> output = p.inputReader().lines().toList(); if (p.waitFor() != 0) throw new IllegalStateException("child failed: " + cmd + "\n" + String.join("\n", output)); return output; } /** The "build": generate the registry, compile it with javac, and pack everything into one JAR (CDS wants JARs). */ static Path buildApp(Path demo, Path out) throws Exception { Path src = Files.createDirectories(out.resolve("gen-src/workbench/container/l03/demo/gen")); Files.writeString(src.resolve("AppRegistry.java"), RegistryGenerator.generate("workbench.container.l03.demo.gen", "AppRegistry", DemoApp.COMPONENTS)); Files.writeString(src.resolve("GeneratedStart.java"), """ package workbench.container.l03.demo.gen; public final class GeneratedStart { public static void main(String[] args) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); String result = workbench.container.l03.demo.app.DemoApp.run(new AppRegistry()); System.out.println(String.format("ready: %s in %.0f ms", result, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6)); } } """); Path genClasses = Files.createDirectories(out.resolve("gen-classes")); int status = ToolProvider.getSystemJavaCompiler().run(null, null, null, "--release", "21", "-proc:none", "-nowarn", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "-d", genClasses.toString(), src.resolve("AppRegistry.java").toString(), src.resolve("GeneratedStart.java").toString()); if (status != 0) throw new IllegalStateException("javac failed on the generated registry"); Path jar = out.resolve("app.jar"); try (OutputStream file = Files.newOutputStream(jar); JarOutputStream zip = new JarOutputStream(file)) { add(zip, demo, "workbench/container/l03/demo"); // the demo app and this class add(zip, location(Container.class), "workbench/container/l03"); // the container, Java half add(zip, location(Interception.class), "workbench/container/l03"); // the container, Kotlin half add(zip, genClasses, "workbench/container/l03/demo/gen"); // what the generator wrote } return jar; } static void add(JarOutputStream zip, Path root, String pkg) throws IOException { try (Stream<Path> files = Files.walk(root.resolve(pkg))) { for (Path f : files.filter(f -> f.toString().endsWith(".class")).sorted().collect(Collectors.toList())) { String name = root.relativize(f).toString().replace('\\', '/'); if (pkg.equals("workbench/container/l03") && name.substring(pkg.length() + 1).contains("/")) continue; // no subpackages zip.putNextEntry(new JarEntry(name)); zip.write(Files.readAllBytes(f)); zip.closeEntry(); } } } static Path location(Class<?> c) throws Exception { return Path.of(c.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation().toURI()); } }

try.expect: On JDK 21 the reflective start loads about 2,200 classes, 814 of them parsed from the Byte Buddy JAR, plus 30 JDK proxies and 3 classes defined from bytes. The generated registry loads about 990 and none of those. Its 51 hidden classes are mostly the lambdas in the generated interceptor classes and the JDK's own. ready and wall differ by machine and run, but the reflective start is several times slower each time. Another JDK version gives other counts; the gap between the two rows is what to look at.

sections.h: Move the wiring to build time: generate the registry
sections.html:
Everything the reflective container works out at start-up depends only on the classes, and the classes are fixed when you build. So do the work then. RegistryGenerator runs the same BeanGraph from lesson 1 at build time: it picks the constructors, orders the graph and checks for cycles, and a cycle now fails the build instead of the deploy. Then it writes a Java class that does the wiring with plain new calls. The lab's test compiles that class with javac, the way a build would.

Each singleton gets a holder class. Lesson 1 promised it:

Java
private static final class FeeCalculator_Holder {
    static final FeeCalculator INSTANCE = new FeeCalculator(FxRates_Holder.INSTANCE);
}
Kotlin
private object FeeCalculatorHolder {
    val INSTANCE = FeeCalculator(FxRatesHolder.INSTANCE)    // a Kotlin object is a holder class too
}

The JVM initializes FeeCalculator_Holder the first time get touches it, once, under the class initialization lock from Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization. Its dependency is another holder, initialized first. There is no volatile, no lock after the first call, and no map: get is a list of if (type == FeeCalculator.class) checks. Prototypes get a factory method instead.

Interceptors become source too. For CardIssuerClient the generator writes HttpIssuerClient_Proxy implements CardIssuerClient, and for SettlementService it writes SettlementService_Intercepted extends SettlementService, the same two models as lesson 2. It reads @Timed and @Retry now and writes their values into the code, INTERCEPTION.chain(true, 3, IssuerUnavailableException.class), so nothing reads an annotation at run time. Quarkus ArC does this with its generated _Subclass classes. Micronaut does the graph work in an annotation processor while javac runs, and Spring's AOT processing generates bean definitions as code ahead of time.

You give up two things. The set of components is fixed when you build: nothing can scan a plugin directory at start-up or choose a bean from an environment variable without code the generator wrote for it. And a holder fails forever. If PaymentService's constructor throws on first use, the JVM marks PaymentService_Holder as failed, and every later get throws NoClassDefFoundError until you restart, where lesson 1's cell would simply try again.

steps: Run GenerateDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It prints the registry the generator writes for the demo app, then tries a graph with a cycle.

PaymentService_Holder reads HttpIssuerClient_Holder (which reads IssuerConfig_Holder), FeeCalculator_Holder, RiskRules_Holder and Ledger_Holder, so the JVM initializes those first, in the order the constructor's arguments are evaluated. settle reaches audit through this, which is the _Intercepted object, so its overriding audit runs the chain before super.audit(p0). The last line is the build fails: Dependency cycle: Payouts -> Statements -> Payouts.

sections.h: Look inside the running container: a histogram and a heap dump
sections.html:
Measure the running container from outside, as Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap did. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram runs a full GC and counts the live objects of every class. Here is the reflective container after one payment, one refund and one payout, trimmed:

 num     #instances         #bytes  class name (module)
 100:            42            672  jdk.proxy2.$Proxy8 (jdk.proxy2)
 145:            13            312  workbench.container.l03.SingletonCell
 176:            14            224  jdk.proxy2.$Proxy2 (jdk.proxy2)
 254:             1            112  net.bytebuddy.dynamic.loading.ByteArrayClassLoader
 523:             1             32  workbench.container.l03.Container
 866:             1             16  jdk.proxy2.$Proxy6 (jdk.proxy2)
 910:             1             16  workbench.container.l03.SettlementService$ByteBuddy$iUqWQUJF

Read it like a ledger. 13 SingletonCells are the 14 components minus the one prototype. One $Proxy6 is the issuer proxy. One ByteArrayClassLoader holds the Byte Buddy subclass and its two helper classes, and one SettlementService$ByteBuddy$... is the bean. The other proxy objects are not beans. In this run $Proxy2, with 14 instances, is the @Component annotation, one instance per component class, and $Proxy8, with 42, is a proxy Byte Buddy uses to call JDK methods that don't exist on every Java version it supports (its JavaDispatcher). There were 119 proxy objects in all, and one of them was a bean.

The histogram says what is alive, not who holds it. jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump <file> writes every object and reference to an HPROF file, 8 MB here. The JVM pauses while it writes, so on a production pod take it when you can afford a pause. In Eclipse MAT, "Path to GC Roots" on the SettlementService$ByteBuddy$... object should lead through SingletonCell.instance and the container's singletons map to the Container, held by a local variable of the main thread.

The demo also proves it by letting go. It drops its only reference to the container and asks for a GC. Byte Buddy's class loader is collected, and with it the generated class: a class keeps its loader alive and an object keeps its class alive, so once the container was unreachable, the whole chain was. The JDK proxy class stays loaded, because it was defined in the application class loader and is cached by Proxy for that loader. The annotation instances stay too, cached with the classes and methods they annotate.

The generated registry has a different root. Its singletons are static fields of holder classes, so they live as long as the class loader that loaded the registry. That is why the lab's tests load a fresh copy of the class for every test.

try.title: Take a histogram and a heap dump of the container
steps: Run RunningContainer with -Pargs=wait added to the command below. It wires the app, makes three calls, prints its pid and two jcmd commands, and waits.
In a second terminal, from labs/, run the two commands it printed. Count the SingletonCells, the ByteArrayClassLoaders and the $ByteBuddy$ instances before you look at the answer.
Optional: open container/build/heapdumps/container.hprof in Eclipse MAT and use "Path to GC Roots" on the SettlementService$ByteBuddy$... object.

Press Enter in the first terminal. It drops the container. Run the histogram command again, then press Enter to end. Without -Pargs=wait, the demo (and its Kotlin twin) runs both jcmd commands itself and prints a shorter, grouped histogram.

code.title: RunningContainer.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l03.demo; import workbench.container.l03.Container; import workbench.container.l03.SettlementService; import workbench.container.l03.demo.app.CardIssuerClient; import workbench.container.l03.demo.app.DemoApp; import java.lang.ref.WeakReference; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Runs the reflective container, then looks inside this JVM with jcmd: a class histogram and a heap * dump. Then it drops the container and checks what the garbage collector could take away. * Run with -Pargs=wait to stop before each step and run jcmd yourself. */ public class RunningContainer { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean wait = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("wait"); long pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid(); Path classes = Path.of(RunningContainer.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation().toURI()); Path dump = Files.createDirectories(classes.getParent().getParent().getParent().resolve("heapdumps")).resolve("container.hprof"); Files.deleteIfExists(dump); // jcmd refuses to overwrite a dump Container container = new Container(DemoApp.COMPONENTS); System.out.println("app: " + DemoApp.run(container)); WeakReference<ClassLoader> generatedLoader = new WeakReference<>(container.get(SettlementService.class).getClass().getClassLoader()); String proxyClass = container.get(CardIssuerClient.class).getClass().getName(); if (wait) { System.out.printf("pid %d. In a second terminal, from labs/:%n", pid); System.out.printf(" jcmd %d GC.class_histogram | grep -E 'workbench|Proxy|ByteBuddy|ByteArray'%n", pid); System.out.printf(" jcmd %d GC.heap_dump %s%n", pid, dump); System.out.println("Then press Enter to drop the container."); System.in.read(); } else { histogram(pid, proxyClass); jcmd(pid, "GC.heap_dump", dump.toString()).forEach(line -> System.out.println("heap dump: " + line)); } container = null; // the only reference to the container for (int i = 0; i < 10 && generatedLoader.get() != null; i++) { System.gc(); // a request; repeat until the loader is gone Thread.sleep(50); } System.out.println("after dropping the container:"); System.out.println(" Byte Buddy's class loader collected: " + (generatedLoader.get() == null)); System.out.println(" " + proxyClass + " still loaded: " + stillLoaded(proxyClass)); if (wait) { System.out.printf("Run the histogram again, then press Enter to exit.%n"); System.in.read(); } else { histogram(pid, proxyClass); } } /** The container's own lines of the histogram, then the proxy classes with live instances, grouped. */ static void histogram(long pid, String ourProxy) throws Exception { List<String> lines = jcmd(pid, "GC.class_histogram"); System.out.println(lines.get(1)); // the column headings lines.stream().filter(l -> l.matches(".*(\\.Container|SingletonCell|InterceptingHandler|SubclassBridge" + "|\\$ByteBuddy\\$\\w+|ByteArrayClassLoader|app\\.PaymentService)( \\(.*)?$") || l.contains(" " + ourProxy + " ")).forEach(System.out::println); int annotations = 0, byteBuddy = 0, others = 0, ours = 0, instances = 0; for (String line : lines) { String[] f = line.trim().split("\\s+"); if (f.length < 4 || !f[3].contains("$Proxy")) continue; // num, #instances, #bytes, class name instances += Integer.parseInt(f[1]); if (f[3].equals(ourProxy)) ours += Integer.parseInt(f[1]); else if (isAnnotation(f[3])) annotations++; else if (f[3].startsWith("net.bytebuddy.")) byteBuddy++; else others++; } System.out.printf(" %d proxy instances: %d annotation proxy classes, %d in Byte Buddy's packages, %d other, %d of ours%n", instances, annotations, byteBuddy, others, ours); } static boolean isAnnotation(String proxyClass) { try { return java.lang.annotation.Annotation.class.isAssignableFrom( Class.forName(proxyClass, false, RunningContainer.class.getClassLoader())); } catch (ClassNotFoundException | LinkageError e) { return false; } } static boolean stillLoaded(String name) { try { Class.forName(name, false, RunningContainer.class.getClassLoader()); // asks the loader, defines nothing return true; } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) { return false; } } static List<String> jcmd(long pid, String... command) throws Exception { List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "jcmd").toString(), Long.toString(pid))); cmd.addAll(List.of(command)); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); List<String> out = p.inputReader().lines().filter(l -> !l.startsWith("Picked up")).toList(); p.waitFor(); return out; } }

Then it drops the container and checks what the garbage collector could take away. // Run with -Pargs=wait to stop before each step and run jcmd yourself. private object Here private var container: Container? = null // the only reference to the container fun main(args: Array<String>) { val wait = args.firstOrNull() == "wait" val pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid() val classes = Path.of(Here::class.java.protectionDomain.codeSource.location.toURI()) val dump = Files.createDirectories(classes.parent.parent.parent.resolve("heapdumps")).resolve("container-kt.hprof") Files.deleteIfExists(dump) // jcmd refuses to overwrite a dump container = Container(DemoApp.COMPONENTS) println("app: " + DemoApp.run(container!!)) val generatedLoader = WeakReference(container!!.get(SettlementService::class.java).javaClass.classLoader) val proxyClass = container!!.get(CardIssuerClient::class.java).javaClass.name if (wait) { println("pid $pid. In a second terminal, from labs/:") println(" jcmd $pid GC.class_histogram | grep -E 'workbench|Proxy|ByteBuddy|ByteArray'") println(" jcmd $pid GC.heap_dump $dump") println("Then press Enter to drop the container.") System.`in`.read() } else { histogram(pid, proxyClass) jcmd(pid, "GC.heap_dump", dump.toString()).forEach { println("heap dump: $it") } } container = null repeat(10) { if (generatedLoader.get() != null) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(50) } // a request; repeat until it is gone } println("after dropping the container:") println(" Byte Buddy's class loader collected: ${generatedLoader.get() == null}") println(" $proxyClass still loaded: ${stillLoaded(proxyClass)}") if (wait) { println("Run the histogram again, then press Enter to exit.") System.`in`.read() } else { histogram(pid, proxyClass) } } /** The container's own lines of the histogram, then the proxy classes with live instances, grouped. */ private fun histogram(pid: Long, ourProxy: String) { val lines = jcmd(pid, "GC.class_histogram") println(lines[1]) // the column headings val ours = Regex(""".*(\.Container|SingletonCell|InterceptingHandler|SubclassBridge|\${'$'}ByteBuddy\${'$'}\w+|ByteArrayClassLoader|app\.PaymentService)( \(.*)?$""") lines.filter { ours.matches(it) || " $ourProxy " in it }.forEach(::println) val proxies = lines.map { it.trim().split(Regex("\\s+")) }.filter { it.size >= 4 && "\$Proxy" in it[3] } val instances = proxies.sumOf { it[1].toInt() } val mine = proxies.filter { it[3] == ourProxy }.sumOf { it[1].toInt() } val others = proxies.map { it[3] }.filter { it != ourProxy } val annotations = others.count(::isAnnotation) val byteBuddy = others.count { !isAnnotation(it) && it.startsWith("net.bytebuddy.") } println(" $instances proxy instances: $annotations annotation proxy classes, $byteBuddy in Byte Buddy's packages, " + "${others.size - annotations - byteBuddy} other, $mine of ours") } private fun isAnnotation(proxyClass: String): Boolean = runCatching { Annotation::class.java.isAssignableFrom(Class.forName(proxyClass, false, Here::class.java.classLoader)) } .getOrDefault(false) private fun stillLoaded(name: String): Boolean = runCatching { Class.forName(name, false, Here::class.java.classLoader) }.isSuccess // asks the loader, defines nothing private fun jcmd(pid: Long, vararg command: String): List<String> { val cmd = listOf(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "jcmd").toString(), pid.toString()) + command val p = ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start() val out = p.inputReader().readLines().filterNot { it.startsWith("Picked up") } p.waitFor() return out }

sections.h: Archive what is left: AppCDS on JDK 21, the AOT cache on JDK 25
sections.html:
Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache showed how to skip parsing and verifying classes at start-up. Apply it to both containers and the last two rows of StartupLadder appear:

reflective, AppCDS            2145      2037       108       544      858
    parsed from byte-buddy.jar 0, JDK proxies 30, defined from bytes 3, hidden 75
generated, AppCDS              882       847        35       143      362
    parsed from byte-buddy.jar 0, JDK proxies 0, defined from bytes 0, hidden 35

AppCDS took Byte Buddy's 814 classes from the archive and nearly halved the reflective start. It could not take the classes made at run time. When the archive was written, JDK 21 printed Skipping jdk/proxy2/$Proxy3: Unsupported location for each of the 30 proxy classes, and the archived run still logs Byte Buddy's three classes as __JVM_DefineClass__: defined from bytes by its own class loader, at every start. So every start still generates and verifies them, and still runs the code that generates them. The generated registry has nothing of the kind: its only run-time classes are 35 hidden ones for lambdas.

The AOT cache on JDK 25 goes further for the classes it can store: they arrive loaded and linked, with profiles from the training run. Use JDK 25.0.4 or later, as that lesson explained. The custom-loader limit stays: as Quarkus's AOT guide puts it, Leyden doesn't support custom class loaders yet, so Byte Buddy's classes are made at every start either way.

The registry is also the shape native image wants (GraalVM native image and Quarkus native). It has no reflection to declare and no classes defined at run time, which a closed world can't contain. That is the whole argument for build-time wiring in one sentence: the less a start has to discover, generate and verify, the more of it a cache, an archive or a native build can do for you.

try.title: Archive both starts
steps: Run StartupLadder once (section 2), so app.jar and classpath.txt exist in container/build/cap4.
Run the two JDK 21 commands. Predict both numbers before you run them: how many classes does the archive refuse, and which run-time classes remain?
If you have JDK 25.0.4 or later, run the last two commands with its java.

code.title: terminal (from labs/)
code.html: # from labs/, after StartupLadder has run once: it wrote app.jar and classpath.txt cd container/build/cap4 CP=$(cat classpath.txt) MAIN=workbench.container.l03.demo.StartupLadder # JDK 21 or later: a dynamic AppCDS archive for the reflective start java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=reflective.jsa -cp "$CP" $MAIN --reflective 2>&1 | grep -c 'Unsupported location' java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=reflective.jsa -Xlog:class+load -cp "$CP" $MAIN --reflective \ | grep -o 'source: __[A-Za-z_]*' | sort | uniq -c # JDK 25.0.4 or later: the one-step AOT cache for the generated registry java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=generated.aot -cp "$CP" workbench.container.l03.demo.gen.GeneratedStart java -XX:AOTCache=generated.aot -Xlog:aot -cp "$CP" workbench.container.l03.demo.gen.GeneratedStart | grep Opened

try.expect: On JDK 21 the first command prints 30: one Unsupported location warning per proxy class. The second prints 3 source: __JVM_DefineClass__, 75 source: __JVM_LookupDefineClass__ and 30 source: __dynamic_proxy__: the Byte Buddy classes, hidden classes and proxies that every start still makes, even with the archive. On JDK 25.0.4 or later the AOT cache commands should end with Opened AOT cache generated.aot. (this course's machine had only JDK 21, so that line comes from the start-up track's runs, not from this app).

analogy: Run-time wiring is a wedding caterer who arrives with raw ingredients and a recipe book, and starts cooking when the guests sit down. It works for any menu, even one changed that morning, and the guests wait. Build-time wiring is the caterer who cooks the day before and only reheats. Dinner is fast, and the menu is fixed the night before: a guest who arrives with a new allergy gets whatever was planned. AppCDS is a faster stove, and it helps both caterers, but only the second one has nothing left to cook. The analogy breaks at freshness: reheated code is exactly as good as fresh, and the JIT still warms it up after the start.
world: This lesson is the reason Quarkus moved its container to build time: ArC does the equivalent of this generator during the Maven build, so your pods start without scanning the class path for beans, and its interceptors are ordinary generated subclasses. The habits that keep that true are concrete. Put configuration a component needs at start-up into build-time properties only when it really is fixed per build. Treat a reflection call or a run-time proxy on the start-up path as a cost you can count with -Xlog:class+load. Read jcmd GC.class_histogram on a running pod before guessing what a container keeps. And when a pod's readiness probe is slow, compare the class count of a cold start before and after the last dependency upgrade.
mistake: The common mistake is measuring the wrong cost. Teams benchmark one proxied call, find a few nanoseconds, and conclude that proxies are free, while the start-up cost (thousands of classes loaded, generated, verified and interpreted before the first request) never appears in a microbenchmark. Others go the other way and remove a proxy from a component that makes one network call a second. People make it because JMH is the tool they know for performance. The fix is to measure both clocks, the way this lesson did: B/op from JMH for the hot path, and -Xlog:class+load counts plus time to the first request for the start, each on its own, before changing anything.

compare.title: A generated registry in Java and the same idea written by hand in Kotlin

java.title: AppRegistry.java (generated, trimmed)
java.html: public final class AppRegistry implements Registry { private static final class FxRates_Holder { static final FxRates INSTANCE = new FxRates(); } private static final class FeeCalculator_Holder { static final FeeCalculator INSTANCE = new FeeCalculator(FxRates_Holder.INSTANCE); } private static PaymentAttempt new_PaymentAttempt() { // a prototype return new PaymentAttempt(FeeCalculator_Holder.INSTANCE); } @Override public <T> T get(Class<T> type) { if (type == FxRates.class) return type.cast(FxRates_Holder.INSTANCE); if (type == FeeCalculator.class) return type.cast(FeeCalculator_Holder.INSTANCE); if (type == PaymentAttempt.class) return type.cast(new_PaymentAttempt()); throw new ContainerException("No component provides " + type.getSimpleName()); } }

kotlin.title: AppRegistry.kt (by hand)
kotlin.html: object AppRegistry { private object FxRatesHolder { val INSTANCE = FxRates() } private object FeeCalculatorHolder { val INSTANCE = FeeCalculator(FxRatesHolder.INSTANCE) } private fun newPaymentAttempt() = PaymentAttempt(FeeCalculatorHolder.INSTANCE) // a prototype @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") fun <T> get(type: Class<T>): T = when (type) { FxRates::class.java -> FxRatesHolder.INSTANCE FeeCalculator::class.java -> FeeCalculatorHolder.INSTANCE PaymentAttempt::class.java -> newPaymentAttempt() else -> throw ContainerException("No component provides ${type.simpleName}") } as T }

compare.note: Both compile to the same mechanism: one class per singleton whose static initializer builds it on first use, under the JVM's class initialization lock. A Kotlin object is that holder class, with its instance in a static INSTANCE field. The difference is who writes it. The Java one comes from a generator and is never edited; the Kotlin one is the kind of code Dagger generates, written by hand, which is fine for ten components and painful for eighty. You don't need by lazy here: it would work, but it adds a Lazy object per bean and a volatile read per access to do what the class initialization lock already does.

worked.title: Design review: where does a feature flag go?

steps.say: A new requirement: in staging, the app must use MockIssuerClient instead of HttpIssuerClient, chosen by the property issuer=mock. In the run-time container it is one filter before the graph is built, because the container learns its components at start-up anyway.
steps.code: List<Class<?>> components = new ArrayList<>(DemoApp.COMPONENTS); if ("mock".equals(System.getProperty("issuer"))) { components.remove(HttpIssuerClient.class); // decided at start-up components.add(MockIssuerClient.class); } Registry registry = new Container(components);

alt.html: val components = DemoApp.COMPONENTS.toMutableList() if (System.getProperty("issuer") == "mock") { components -= HttpIssuerClient::class.java // decided at start-up components += MockIssuerClient::class.java } val registry: Registry = Container(components)

steps.say: The generated registry has no start-up graph to change. One option is to generate one registry per profile and choose at the edge of the program. Each registry stays plain code, and the flag picks a class, not a graph.
steps.code: String source = RegistryGenerator.generate("com.acme.gen", "StagingRegistry", stagingComponents); // ...and ProductionRegistry from the production list, both at build time Registry registry = "mock".equals(System.getProperty("issuer")) ? new StagingRegistry() : new ProductionRegistry();

alt.html: val source = RegistryGenerator.generate("com.acme.gen", "StagingRegistry", stagingComponents) // ...and ProductionRegistry from the production list, both at build time val registry: Registry = if (System.getProperty("issuer") == "mock") StagingRegistry() else ProductionRegistry()

steps.say: Check the costs. Two registries double the generated code and ship the mock in the production artifact. If the flag really is fixed per environment, a build-time property is cleaner: build the staging image with the staging list. Quarkus draws exactly this line between build-time configuration, fixed in the artifact, and run-time configuration, read at start-up.

Write the decision down in one sentence a reviewer can check: "The issuer implementation is chosen per build, so each image wires one graph; a run-time property may change the issuer's URL and timeouts, never which class is wired." That sentence is the design review's answer, and the test that proves it is the lab's: the generated registry wires the same graph as the reflective one, for each list.

lab.title: Generate the registry
steps: Run the tests once. All seven fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Everything else in l03 is the finished container from lessons 1 and 2, plus Registry (what both containers offer) and ProxySource, which writes the interceptor classes as source. Skim ProxySource.emit once.
Read GeneratedCode in the test folder: it is the "build". It compiles your source with javac and loads it in a fresh class loader for every test, so each test gets fresh singletons.

In RegistryGenerator.generate, build a BeanGraph, take its creation order, and start with header(...). For each component, write a holder class for a singleton or a factory method for a prototype, using the helpers holder, factory, beanType and newExpression.
Write get: for each component, one if (type == X.class) return type.cast(...) line per type in boundTypes(graph, c), using reference(c). End with the throw line and footer(order).
Run the tests until all seven pass. If one says the generated source does not compile, read the numbered listing it prints. Then run GenerateDemo and read what your code writes for the demo app.
hints: Write class names with getCanonicalName(). getName() gives WiringTest$Payouts for a nested class, which javac reads as a class named with a dollar sign, not as a nested class.
Container.scopeOf(c) is package-private in Container, and RegistryGenerator is in the same package, so you can call it.

The concurrency test passes as soon as your holders are right, with no lock in your code. If you can say why (one thread runs a class's static initializer while the others wait), you have the main idea of this lesson.
A test that sees NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class ...Holder means a constructor threw inside a holder. The first failure in the output names the real exception.
lab.done: All seven tests in BuildTimeTest pass, and GenerateDemo prints a registry whose PaymentService_Holder uses four other holders.

drill.title: A holder-based registry by hand
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Without a generator, write a registry for three components: FxRates() (singleton), FeeCalculator(FxRates) (singleton) and Quote(FeeCalculator) (prototype), with a get(Class<T>) that throws for anything else. Then compare. Which line makes FeeCalculator safe when eight threads ask first?

answer.html: public final class FeeRegistry { private static final class FxRatesHolder { static final FxRates INSTANCE = new FxRates(); } private static final class FeeCalculatorHolder { // initialized once, under the JVM's lock static final FeeCalculator INSTANCE = new FeeCalculator(FxRatesHolder.INSTANCE); } private static Quote newQuote() { // a prototype: new every time return new Quote(FeeCalculatorHolder.INSTANCE); } public <T> T get(Class<T> type) { if (type == FxRates.class) return type.cast(FxRatesHolder.INSTANCE); if (type == FeeCalculator.class) return type.cast(FeeCalculatorHolder.INSTANCE); if (type == Quote.class) return type.cast(newQuote()); throw new IllegalArgumentException("No component provides " + type.getSimpleName()); } }

alt.html: object FeeRegistry { private object FxRatesHolder { val INSTANCE = FxRates() } private object FeeCalculatorHolder { val INSTANCE = FeeCalculator(FxRatesHolder.INSTANCE) } // once, under the JVM's lock private fun newQuote() = Quote(FeeCalculatorHolder.INSTANCE) // a prototype: new every time @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") fun <T> get(type: Class<T>): T = when (type) { FxRates::class.java -> FxRatesHolder.INSTANCE FeeCalculator::class.java -> FeeCalculatorHolder.INSTANCE Quote::class.java -> newQuote() else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("No component provides ${type.simpleName}") } as T }

recap: Measure both clocks. JMH's -prof gc gave 0 B/op for a direct call and for generated interceptor code (escape analysis removed its objects), 160 for a Byte Buddy subclass and 208 for a JDK proxy. Per call, that only matters in hot loops.

At start-up the reflective container loaded 2,207 classes against 991 for generated wiring: 814 from Byte Buddy's JAR, 30 JDK proxy classes (mostly annotation instances), 3 generated subclasses and helpers, and over a hundred hidden classes.

A generated registry does the graph work at build time and wires with new: a holder class per singleton (lazy and thread-safe through the class initialization lock), a factory per prototype, identity checks in get, and interceptors as source. A cycle fails the build; a failing holder fails until restart.

jcmd GC.class_histogram shows what the container keeps alive; a heap dump and MAT's path to GC roots show who holds it. Dropping the container freed Byte Buddy's loader and classes; the JDK proxy class and annotation instances stayed.

AppCDS and the AOT cache archive classes from JARs, not classes made at run time: the 30 proxies are skipped and Byte Buddy's classes come from a custom loader. Generated wiring leaves almost nothing to make at start-up, which also suits native image.

explain.prompt: Design review. A sceptical reviewer says: "Our Spring Boot services wire everything by reflection and proxies at start-up, and it works. Generating code is extra build machinery. Why should we ever wire at build time?" Defend the design you built across these three lessons, with the numbers you measured, and say when you would not do it.
explain.answer: Both containers compute the same thing: the same constructors, the same order, the same interceptor chains. The only question is when. At run time it costs every start: here 2,207 classes against 991, because the container loads Byte Buddy, reads annotations through proxies, generates and verifies subclasses, and runs all of it cold in the interpreter. AppCDS halved that, but it can't archive the proxies or Byte Buddy's classes, so every start still generates them. Generated wiring moves the work to the build: a cycle fails the build, the start runs only holder initializers, the per-call path allocates nothing after inlining, and the result has no reflection for native image to declare. What it costs: a generator in the build, a component set fixed per artifact, and holders that fail permanently if a constructor throws, so constructors must be trivial. I wouldn't do it for a long-running service that starts once a week and needs plugins or beans chosen at run time; there, reflection's flexibility is worth a slower start. I would for services that scale out often, run as many small instances, or must start inside a tight readiness budget, which is most of what we deploy to Kubernetes.

deeper.html:
What a production container adds to the one you built, roughly in the order you would need it:

  • Lifecycle callbacks: @PostConstruct after injection and @PreDestroy on shutdown, run in reverse creation order so a Ledger closes after the PaymentService that writes to it.
  • Qualifiers (@Named, @Qualifier) for two implementations of one interface, and resolution by generic type, so Repository<Payment> and Repository<Refund> are different dependencies.
  • More scopes: per request, per session, per Kafka message, with a client proxy that forwards to the right instance for the current scope.
  • Configuration injection, with type conversion and validation, split into build-time and run-time properties.
  • Interceptor ordering by priority, decorators, and events between components.
  • Lookup injection (Provider<T>, Instance<T>) for edges that must be followed at call time.
  • Test support: replacing one component with a mock without rewriting the graph.
  • Error messages that print the whole dependency path, not only the cycle.

The way the generator runs matters too. This lab runs it as a separate step on compiled classes, which is close to what Quarkus does during its build. Dagger and Micronaut run theirs as annotation processors inside javac, so the generated classes are compiled with your code and IDEs can show them, but the processor sees source-level elements instead of loaded classes. Spring's AOT processing starts the application context during the build and writes what it found as code.

For the start itself, the next levers after this lesson are the ones the start-up track covered: an AOT cache trained on representative traffic, then native image if memory per instance or start time is still the limit. Generated wiring makes both of them easier, because there is less left for the JVM to discover.
